"abstract": "A prospective cohort of 2163 collegiate athletes with a concussion, from the CARE Consortium, in which 47.0% reported new or worsened neck pain after injury. Neck pain was associated with female sex, altered mental status, contact level and injury mechanism, and with longer symptom duration, while return-to-play protocol length did not differ.",

-   "tldr": "About half of collegiate athletes with a concussion report new or worsened neck pain, and those athletes had about 2 extra days of symptoms. The return-to-play protocol was no longer for them.",

+   "tldr": "About half of collegiate athletes with a concussion report new or worsened neck pain, and those athletes had about 2 more days of symptoms on average. The length of the return-to-play protocol did not differ between groups.",

"methods": "Secondary analysis of the prospective CARE Consortium cohort (2014-2018) with NCAA varsity and military service academy athletes. Neck pain was rated on the SCAT3 at baseline and after injury, and was compared with preinjury baseline. Bivariate tests were followed by forward stepwise logistic regression, and recovery outcomes were compared with Wilcoxon and chi-square tests.",

"findings": "Of 2163 athletes, 1016 (47.0%) reported new or worsened neck pain. In the regression, female sex (OR 1.48), altered mental status (OR 1.28), higher contact level (collision vs contact OR 1.42), and mechanism and object collided with were associated with neck pain. Those with neck pain had a mean symptom duration of 11.1 vs 8.8 days (P < .001), were less likely to resolve symptoms in 7 days, and had no difference in return-to-play protocol length (7.5 vs 7.4 days, P = .592).",

"limitations": "Neck pain severity was missing for 267 athletes, there were no objective cervical assessments, and new pain was not analysed separately from worsened pain. Sex was not significant in the bivariate comparison (P = .117), and the sex association comes from the regression and a post hoc subsample. The model used forward stepwise selection with many candidate variables, and the findings are associations, not causes.",

The data support monitoring symptom duration in these athletes, but they do not establish that cervical treatment shortens recovery.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Not applicable as a performance study. The finding is useful for return-to-activity planning, since athletes with neck pain after a concussion had more symptomatic days and longer time to normal academic performance.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The paper shows that athletes with new or worsened neck pain after a concussion had longer symptom duration and time to normal academic performance, but the return-to-play protocol length did not differ. "practicalImplications": "The authors recommend a cervical spine examination for concussed athletes who report neck pain.    "athleteDev": "Performance Application: This is not a performance study.    "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The return-to-play protocol length did not differ by neck pain status (7.5 vs 7.4 days, P = .592), so the paper does not show that neck pain changes return-to-play timing. Article history:                                         Objectives: Hamstring injuries are common among soccer players. The hamstring outcome score (HaOS)
Received 10 January 2020                                 might be useful to identify amateur players at risk of hamstring injury. Therefore the aims of this study
Received in revised form 25 August 2020                  were: To determine the association between the HaOS and prior and new hamstring injuries in amateur
Accepted 3 January 2021
                                                         soccer players, and to determine the prognostic value of the HaOS for identifying players with or without
Available online xxx
                                                         previous hamstring injuries at risk of future injury.
                                                         Design: Cohort study.
Keywords:
                                                         Methods: HaOS scores and information about previous injuries were collected at baseline and new injuries
Hamstring injury
Soccer
                                                         were prospectively registered during a cluster-randomized controlled trial involving 400 amateur soccer
Football                                                 players. Analysis of variance and t-tests were used to determine the association between the HaOS and
Prevention                                               previous and new hamstring injury, respectively. Logistic regression analysis indicated the prognostic
Prognostic value                                         value of the HaOS for predicting new hamstring injuries.
Injury risk                                              Results: Analysis of data of 356 players indicated that lower HaOS scores were associated with more
                                                         previous hamstring injuries (F = 17.4; p = 0.000) and that players with lower HaOS scores sustained more
                                                         new hamstring injuries (T = 3.59, df = 67.23, p = 0.001). With a conventional HaOS score cut-off of 80%,
                                                         logistic regression models yielded a probability of hamstring injuries of 11%, 18%, and 28% for players
                                                         with 0,1, or 2 hamstring injuries in the previous season, respectively.
                                                         Conclusions: The HaOS is associated with previous and future hamstring injury and might be a useful tool
                                                         to provide players with insight into their risk of sustaining a new hamstring injury risk when used in
                                                         combination with previous injuries.

19	  Abstract
20	  Background Previous research has demonstrated a relationship between modifiable (e.g. hamstring strength,
21	  muscle fascicle length and high-speed running load), non-modifiable factors (e.g. age, previous injury) and hamstring
22	  strain injury (HSI) risk. However, these factors have mostly been assessed in isolation and no study to date has
23	  investigated the associations between running load, strength and muscle architecture with HSI risk. The study aim
24	  was to explore the interactions between modifiable HSI risk factors that are commonly assessed within elite Australian
25	  footballers.
26	  Methods A prospective cohort study design. Eccentric knee flexor strength and biceps femoris long head (BFlh)
27	  fascicle lengths were measured in 299 unique elite-level Australian Football players (age 24 ± 4 years, height
28	  188 ± 8 cm, and weight 87 ± 9 kg) during two pre-seasons. Data from wearable micro-sensor units (high-speed
29	  running at ≥ 24k/hr and total distance) were collected over two seasons of elite Australian Football.
30	  Results Across 408 player-seasons there were 67 HSIs (16.4%), which took an average of 17 ± 10 days and 23 ± 12
31	  days to return to full training and competitive matches, respectively. Univariate analysis showed that BFlh pennation
32	  angle (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.2), fascicle length (OR 0.6, 95% CI 0.5–0.9), weekly high-speed running distance (OR 1.7,
33	  95% CI 1.2–2.4), weekly change in total distance (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–2.2) and weekly change in high-speed running
34	  distance (OR 1.6, 1.2–2.2) were significantly different between the injured and uninjured group (P < 0.05). Combining
35	  strength and architectural variables of BFlh pennation angle, fascicle length and peak force was able to explain 12% of
36	  variance in the risk of sustaining a HSI. The addition of running load exposure variables of weekly distance and change
37	  in weekly distance to the multivariate model increased the explained variance to 20%.

The Relationship Between Running Load,
Strength, Muscle Architecture and Hamstring
Strain Injury Across Two Seasons of Elite Male
Australian Football: A Prospective Cohort
Study
Ray Breed1,2,4,9* , David A. Opar2,4 , Rich D. Johnston3,4,5 , Jack T. Hickey4,6 , Morgan D. Williams7,8,
Nirav Maniar2,4 and Ryan G. Timmins3,4


  Abstract
  Background Previous research has demonstrated a relationship between modifiable (e.g. hamstring strength,
  muscle fascicle length and high-speed running load), non-modifiable factors (e.g. age, previous injury) and hamstring
  strain injury (HSI) risk. However, these factors have mostly been assessed in isolation and no study to date has
  investigated the associations between running load, strength and muscle architecture with HSI risk. The study aim
  was to explore the interactions between modifiable HSI risk factors that are commonly assessed within elite Australian
  footballers.
  Methods A prospective cohort study design. Eccentric knee flexor strength and biceps femoris long head (BFlh)
  fascicle lengths were measured in 299 unique elite-level Australian Football players (age 24 ± 4 years, height
  188 ± 8 cm, and weight 87 ± 9 kg) during two pre-seasons. Data from wearable micro-sensor units (high-speed
  running at ≥ 24k/hr and total distance) were collected over two seasons of elite Australian Football.
  Results Across 408 player-seasons there were 67 HSIs (16.4%), which took an average of 17 ± 10 days and 23 ± 12
  days to return to full training and competitive matches, respectively. Univariate analysis showed that BFlh pennation
  angle (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.2), fascicle length (OR 0.6, 95% CI 0.5–0.9), weekly high-speed running distance (OR 1.7,
  95% CI 1.2–2.4), weekly change in total distance (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–2.2) and weekly change in high-speed running
  distance (OR 1.6, 1.2–2.2) were significantly different between the injured and uninjured group (P < 0.05). Combining
  strength and architectural variables of BFlh pennation angle, fascicle length and peak force was able to explain 12% of
  variance in the risk of sustaining a HSI. The addition of running load exposure variables of weekly distance and change
  in weekly distance to the multivariate model increased the explained variance to 20%.

 Conclusion Combining measures of running load exposure with hamstring strength and architecture, increases the
 variance explained by multivariate models for determining HSI risk. Despite this, there was still approximately 80% of
 unexplained variance in sustaining a HSI in this study.
 Key Points
    • 	 Running load, eccentric knee flexor strength and biceps femoris long head (BFlh) architectural variables were
        measured in this study, with pennation angle, fascicle length, weekly high-speed running, weekly change in total
        distance and weekly change in high-speed running each having a significant association with HSI risk (P < 0.05)
        in isolation.
    • 	 Multivariate modelling showed that a combination of five variables of BFlh pennation angle and fascicle length,
        eccentric knee flexor strength, weekly distance and weekly change in distance had the strongest association with
        HSI risk.
    • 	 However, these variables when combined only explained ~ 20% of the variance, leaving 80% of the difference
        between injured and non-injured players unexplained by the variables measured in this study.

258	                           2. Pathophysiology of OTS
259	                                 In general, regular exercise of mild to moderate intensity is used as a non-pharmacological
260	                           intervention strategy to prevent various pathological medical conditions such as type
261	                           2 diabetes, insulin resistance, pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases, colon cancer and
262	                           breast cancer, dementia, and depression, and to improve the symptoms [20–26]. Despite
263	                           this, it is necessary to highlight the paradox of the overtrained athlete; as already stated,
264	                           excessive training can aggravate the decline in sports performance [20,27]. Numerous
265	                           theories on the causes of this phenomenon have been proposed and studied.
266	
267	                           2.1. Cytokine Hypothesis
268	                                 In addition to the association between overtraining and skeletal muscle injury that
269	                           was established about two decades ago, the cytokine hypothesis was introduced, which
270	                           integrates and explains most of the signs and symptoms that appear to be linked to
271	                           the decline in sports performance induced by excessive training [11,21,28]. Therefore,
272	                           the hypothesis states that high-load training associated with insufficient recovery could
273	                           induce musculoskeletal trauma and subsequently determine the production and release of
274	                           cytokines and interleukins such as IL-1 beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha with subsequent multi-
275	                           organ interaction [11,12]. This theory has been extensively studied through various works
276	                           in multiple fields. For example, elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-alpha in skeletal muscle
277	                           have been shown in mouse studies to be related to impairment of the insulin signaling
278	                           pathway, resulting in insulin resistance, muscle atrophy, and activation of endoplasmic
279	                           reticulum (ER) stress [20,29]. Furthermore, high levels of cytokines such as IL-1 beta,
280	                           IL-6, and TNF-alpha, derived from peripheral inflammatory stimuli, at the hypothalamic
281	                           level are linked to an increased restriction of food intake among the cytokines. TNF-
282	                           alpha plays a fundamental role in reduced food intake and increased cellular catabolism,
283	                           causing difficulty in increasing body weight [30–34]. Furthermore, based on the theoretical
284	                           correlation between inflammation and ER stress [29], a study by Pinto et al. states that the
285	                           activation of hypothalamic ER stress is present above all following excessive training [35].
286	                           These data strengthen the theory of proinflammatory cytokines, as they could act as an
287	                           initial stimulus in the central nervous system, inducing some maladaptation soon after a
288	                           period of excessive training, affecting physical performance, food restriction, and cellular
289	                           catabolism [36]. Finally, the inflammatory role of cytokines may also be linked to the
290	                           development of pathological cardiac hypertrophy, due to the increase in IL-6 [31]. Indeed,
291	                           recently, there has been an increase in IL-6 protein levels, a reduction in the activation
292	                           of AMPK-activated protein kinase, mTOR, and ribosomal protein rpS6, and signs of left
293	                           ventricular fibrosis in mice [37]. The results suggest that excessive training can induce
294	                           signs of pathological cardiac hypertrophy, thus contributing to impairment and reduction
295	                           in physical performance [37]. Thus, it is difficult for athletes to manage and recover by
296	                           modulating overtraining at a systemic level due to the proinflammatory action of cytokines.
297	
298	                           2.2. Glutamine Hypothesis
299	                                The production of cytokines is not the only reason for the onset of overtraining syn-
300	                           drome; there is also a relationship between hormones and overtraining syndrome, the latter
301	                           of which can lead to complex hormonal dysfunctions [3]. Nonetheless, the diagnosis of OTS
302	                           is complicated and can only be made after the exclusion of other more common medical
303	                           conditions. Physiological, biochemical, and immunological markers for overtraining have
304	                           received much attention in recent years and could be of potential use if routinely measured
305	                           in the laboratory as a medical aid in preventing overtraining [38]. Glutamine is among
306	                           the various molecules that could be used as biomarkers of overtraining. Glutamine is
307	                           an essential amino acid for the function of immune cells, in particular [4,12,39]. It also
308	                           plays a key role in DNA and RNA synthesis, nitrogen transport, and acid–base balance
309	                           and gluconeogenesis [4,13,39]. The decrease in glutamine after physical exercise could be
310	                           responsible for an increase in the incidence of infections of the respiratory system and of
311	                           the upper respiratory tract (URTI) in overtrained athletes [4,11,40]. Prolonged training
312	 Nutrients 2023, 15, 4916                                                                                            4 of 18
313	
314	
315	
316	
317	                           or repeated periods of high-intensity training could transiently reduce plasma glutamine
318	                           concentrations, resulting in greater sensitivity to URTIs [11,13,39]. As described in the
319	                           cytokine theory, plasma glutamine also plays a key role in various processes controlled
320	                           by cytokines [41]. Glutamine is a molecular precursor of the synthesis of inflammatory
321	                           proteins which are upregulated with overtraining [12]. Furthermore, systemic inflamma-
322	                           tion, given by the increase in proinflammatory cytokines, induces a catabolic state with
323	                           a consequent increase in both glucose and protein metabolism. Therefore, glutamine is a
324	                           crucial element in gluconeogenesis. Furthermore, alterations in the hypothalamic–pituitary–
325	                           adrenal (HPA) and gonadal (HPG) axis, following some studies in the literature, appear
326	                           to be responsible for OTS. In particular, endurance athletes might show subtle changes in
327	                           HPA axis function and thus show alterations in the levels of cortisol, ACTH, testosterone,
328	                           and other hormones [42–45]. In a study by Barron et al., an adrenocortical deficit was also
329	                           highlighted in athletes with overtraining syndrome [44]. That is, the data show that growth
330	                           hormone, prolactin, and ACTH responses to insulin-induced hypoglycemia were lower in
331	                           overtrained athletes than in healthy, well-trained controls. Unfortunately, however, current
332	                           data and research are in some cases inconsistent regarding the patterns of these hormonal
333	                           changes, as they depend on various factors including individual training capacity, intrinsic
334	                           vulnerability to stressful factors, and other hormonal levels [45].
335	
336	                           2.3. Central Fatigue Theory
337	                                 OTS is often characterized by mood, sleep–wake cycle, and behavioral disturbances [15,
338	                           43,46,47]. The neurotransmitter involved in the regulation of these mechanisms is serotonin
339	                           (5-HT); 5-HT alterations could trigger OTS [3,12,46–48]. Central fatigue theory hypothesizes
340	                           that OTS is caused by an increase in the synthesis of 5-hydroxytryptomine (5-HT) in the
341	                           central nervous system (CNS). Physical exercise decreases the levels of branched-chain
342	                           amino acids (BCAA) due to an increase in their oxidation into glucose, favoring the entry
343	                           of tryptophan into the brain and the subsequent conversion into 5-HT as both BCAAs
344	                           and tryptophan use the same transporter to cross the blood–brain barrier [48]. Therefore,
345	                           a decrease in plasma BCAAs with a consequent increase in plasma tryptophan lead to
346	                           an increase in CNS tryptophan levels [43,48]. 5-HT derives from tryptophan. Budgett
347	                           et al. studied how the administration of serotonin reuptake inhibitors to athletes increases
348	                           the levels of 5-HT with consequent reduction in the athletes’ performance [48], while the
349	                           integration of branched-chain amino acids therefore reduced 5-HT production and resulted
350	                           in increased physical and mental energy [49].
351	
352	                           2.4. Glycogen Hypothesis
353	                                Another phenomenon that could interfere with an alteration of the central neuro-
354	                           transmitters involved in fatigue during OTS could be a reduction in muscle glycogen
355	                           due to overtraining [50]. Glycogen is the key energy source during moderate to vigorous
356	                           exercise [50]. Low muscle glycogen also results in an increase in oxidative processes and
357	                           a decrease in total concentrations of BCAA, as reported, leading to central fatigue [50].
358	                           Some studies report that, during OTS, there are lower amounts of lactate in the blood in
359	                           overtrained athletes compared to well-trained athletes [51,52]. Therefore, post-exercise
360	                           blood lactate measurement could be used as a tool to identify athletes at risk of overtraining,
361	                           especially if such testing were performed on a regular basis [51,52].
362	
363	                           2.5. Autonomic Nervous System Hypothesis
364	                                Certainly, an imbalance in the autonomic nervous system, reducing sympathetic
365	                           activation and parasympathetic dominance, could lead to some symptoms of OTS such
366	                           as decreased performance, fatigue, depression, and bradycardia, but also to a reduced
367	                           nocturnal urinary excretion of catecholamines [4,12,43]. Generally, catecholamine excretion
368	                           decreases with increasing training and fatigue, returning to baseline levels during the
369	                           recovery period [4,53]. A reduced organ sensitivity to catecholamines could therefore be
370	                           an indicator of symptoms of reduced sympathetic activation [43]. Furthermore, studies
371	 Nutrients 2023, 15, 4916                                                                                             5 of 18
372	
373	
374	
375	
376	                           have stated that the effects of intense training on autonomic nervous system control may
377	                           be reversible, even after a week of rest [54]. Heart rate variability (HRV) monitoring could
378	                           therefore be an indicator of autonomic function and a predictor of overtraining [45,55].
379	
380	                           2.6. Oxidative Stress Hypothesis
381	                                 Intense physical exercise could generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) and conse-
382	                           quently increase oxidative stress [56]. ROS are related to post-exercise inflammatory
383	                           response mechanisms and to the propagation of muscle damage with promotion of ROS-
384	                           induced infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages into muscle [57,58]. Neutrophils and
385	                           macrophages generate a free radical such as superoxide, which in turn can be converted
386	                           into hydrogen peroxide, which is then able to react with the superoxide in the presence
387	                           of a transition metal to form hydroxyl radicals [58]. Furthermore, the typical markers of
388	                           protein oxidation and the total oxidizing capacity were elevated, while the levels of an-
389	                           tioxidants such as glutathione and coenzyme Q10, and γ-tocopherol and carotenoids were
390	                           decreased [59–61]. Alterations in redox homeostasis have also been reported in individuals
391	                           with OTS; however, information on ROS generation in OTS needs further research. The
392	                           identification of common biomarkers for overtrained athletes could allow an adequate in-
393	                           tervention to prevent the progression of fatigue towards a more severe stage of overtraining
394	                           syndrome [59–61].
395	
396	                           3. Dietary Intake in OTS
397	                                Overtraining syndrome, and therefore an imbalance between training and recovery,
398	                           can be aggravated or implied by improper nutritional intake [62–64]. Nutrition therefore
399	                           plays a fundamental role in maintaining correct body homeostasis, as an imbalance in
400	                           the quantities and proportions of macro- and micronutrients, but also an incorrect state
401	                           of hydration, could affect correct energy intake, the maintenance of normal physiological
402	                           functions, and good body composition, necessary for recovery [5]. However, there are
403	                           few studies in the literature on the relationship between nutrition and OTS. Some of the
404	                           published studies state that inadequate nutrition, pathologies, and stress factors and sleep
405	                           disorders [65] can lead to dysfunctions of the normal metabolic processes involved in im-
406	                           mune, inflammatory, neurological, hormonal, and metabolic responses [65]. For example,
407	                           it has already been demonstrated that overtraining syndrome can reduce an athlete’s ap-
408	                           petite, producing a counterproductive effect, since if the athlete presents continuous caloric
409	                           deficits during training, these could elevate both the stress hormone and the response
410	                           and production of cytokines during physical exercise, limiting the athlete [11,12,66–70].
411	                           Furthermore, fatigue, injury, immunosuppression, and decreased performance can occur
412	                           not only when energy expenditure regularly exceeds daily caloric intake but also when
413	                           hydration is insufficient [70–72]. In fact, incorrect hydration could have a negative effect not
414	                           only on performance but also on the metabolism of some macronutrients, such as glycogen,
415	                           which can only be stored in the muscle when bound to water in a ratio of 1:3 g [72]. It has
416	                           been found that even low levels of dehydration can compromise both the athlete’s exercise
417	                           capacity and the cardiovascular and thermoregulatory responses [73]. Optimal perfor-
418	                           mance, therefore, is possible only when dehydration as well as hyperthermia is minimized
419	                           by ingesting large volumes of fluids during exercise. Therefore, the consumption of liquids

                           2. Pathophysiology of OTS
                                 In general, regular exercise of mild to moderate intensity is used as a non-pharmacological
                           intervention strategy to prevent various pathological medical conditions such as type
                           2 diabetes, insulin resistance, pulmonary and cardiovascular diseases, colon cancer and
                           breast cancer, dementia, and depression, and to improve the symptoms [20–26]. Despite
                           this, it is necessary to highlight the paradox of the overtrained athlete; as already stated,
                           excessive training can aggravate the decline in sports performance [20,27]. Numerous
                           theories on the causes of this phenomenon have been proposed and studied.

                           2.1. Cytokine Hypothesis
                                 In addition to the association between overtraining and skeletal muscle injury that
                           was established about two decades ago, the cytokine hypothesis was introduced, which
                           integrates and explains most of the signs and symptoms that appear to be linked to
                           the decline in sports performance induced by excessive training [11,21,28]. Therefore,
                           the hypothesis states that high-load training associated with insufficient recovery could
                           induce musculoskeletal trauma and subsequently determine the production and release of
                           cytokines and interleukins such as IL-1 beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha with subsequent multi-
                           organ interaction [11,12]. This theory has been extensively studied through various works
                           in multiple fields. For example, elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-alpha in skeletal muscle
                           have been shown in mouse studies to be related to impairment of the insulin signaling
                           pathway, resulting in insulin resistance, muscle atrophy, and activation of endoplasmic
                           reticulum (ER) stress [20,29]. Furthermore, high levels of cytokines such as IL-1 beta,
                           IL-6, and TNF-alpha, derived from peripheral inflammatory stimuli, at the hypothalamic
                           level are linked to an increased restriction of food intake among the cytokines. TNF-
                           alpha plays a fundamental role in reduced food intake and increased cellular catabolism,
                           causing difficulty in increasing body weight [30–34]. Furthermore, based on the theoretical
                           correlation between inflammation and ER stress [29], a study by Pinto et al. states that the
                           activation of hypothalamic ER stress is present above all following excessive training [35].
                           These data strengthen the theory of proinflammatory cytokines, as they could act as an
                           initial stimulus in the central nervous system, inducing some maladaptation soon after a
                           period of excessive training, affecting physical performance, food restriction, and cellular
                           catabolism [36]. Finally, the inflammatory role of cytokines may also be linked to the
                           development of pathological cardiac hypertrophy, due to the increase in IL-6 [31]. Indeed,
                           recently, there has been an increase in IL-6 protein levels, a reduction in the activation
                           of AMPK-activated protein kinase, mTOR, and ribosomal protein rpS6, and signs of left
                           ventricular fibrosis in mice [37]. The results suggest that excessive training can induce
                           signs of pathological cardiac hypertrophy, thus contributing to impairment and reduction
                           in physical performance [37]. Thus, it is difficult for athletes to manage and recover by
                           modulating overtraining at a systemic level due to the proinflammatory action of cytokines.

                           2.2. Glutamine Hypothesis
                                The production of cytokines is not the only reason for the onset of overtraining syn-
                           drome; there is also a relationship between hormones and overtraining syndrome, the latter
                           of which can lead to complex hormonal dysfunctions [3]. Nonetheless, the diagnosis of OTS
                           is complicated and can only be made after the exclusion of other more common medical
                           conditions. Physiological, biochemical, and immunological markers for overtraining have
                           received much attention in recent years and could be of potential use if routinely measured
                           in the laboratory as a medical aid in preventing overtraining [38]. Glutamine is among
                           the various molecules that could be used as biomarkers of overtraining. Glutamine is
                           an essential amino acid for the function of immune cells, in particular [4,12,39]. It also
                           plays a key role in DNA and RNA synthesis, nitrogen transport, and acid–base balance
                           and gluconeogenesis [4,13,39]. The decrease in glutamine after physical exercise could be
                           responsible for an increase in the incidence of infections of the respiratory system and of
                           the upper respiratory tract (URTI) in overtrained athletes [4,11,40]. Prolonged training
 Nutrients 2023, 15, 4916                                                                                            4 of 18




                           or repeated periods of high-intensity training could transiently reduce plasma glutamine
                           concentrations, resulting in greater sensitivity to URTIs [11,13,39]. As described in the
                           cytokine theory, plasma glutamine also plays a key role in various processes controlled
                           by cytokines [41]. Glutamine is a molecular precursor of the synthesis of inflammatory
                           proteins which are upregulated with overtraining [12]. Furthermore, systemic inflamma-
                           tion, given by the increase in proinflammatory cytokines, induces a catabolic state with
                           a consequent increase in both glucose and protein metabolism. Therefore, glutamine is a
                           crucial element in gluconeogenesis. Furthermore, alterations in the hypothalamic–pituitary–
                           adrenal (HPA) and gonadal (HPG) axis, following some studies in the literature, appear
                           to be responsible for OTS. In particular, endurance athletes might show subtle changes in
                           HPA axis function and thus show alterations in the levels of cortisol, ACTH, testosterone,
                           and other hormones [42–45]. In a study by Barron et al., an adrenocortical deficit was also
                           highlighted in athletes with overtraining syndrome [44]. That is, the data show that growth
                           hormone, prolactin, and ACTH responses to insulin-induced hypoglycemia were lower in
                           overtrained athletes than in healthy, well-trained controls. Unfortunately, however, current
                           data and research are in some cases inconsistent regarding the patterns of these hormonal
                           changes, as they depend on various factors including individual training capacity, intrinsic
                           vulnerability to stressful factors, and other hormonal levels [45].

                           2.3. Central Fatigue Theory
                                 OTS is often characterized by mood, sleep–wake cycle, and behavioral disturbances [15,
                           43,46,47]. The neurotransmitter involved in the regulation of these mechanisms is serotonin
                           (5-HT); 5-HT alterations could trigger OTS [3,12,46–48]. Central fatigue theory hypothesizes
                           that OTS is caused by an increase in the synthesis of 5-hydroxytryptomine (5-HT) in the
                           central nervous system (CNS). Physical exercise decreases the levels of branched-chain
                           amino acids (BCAA) due to an increase in their oxidation into glucose, favoring the entry
                           of tryptophan into the brain and the subsequent conversion into 5-HT as both BCAAs
                           and tryptophan use the same transporter to cross the blood–brain barrier [48]. Therefore,
                           a decrease in plasma BCAAs with a consequent increase in plasma tryptophan lead to
                           an increase in CNS tryptophan levels [43,48]. 5-HT derives from tryptophan. Budgett
                           et al. studied how the administration of serotonin reuptake inhibitors to athletes increases
                           the levels of 5-HT with consequent reduction in the athletes’ performance [48], while the
                           integration of branched-chain amino acids therefore reduced 5-HT production and resulted
                           in increased physical and mental energy [49].

                           2.4. Glycogen Hypothesis
                                Another phenomenon that could interfere with an alteration of the central neuro-
                           transmitters involved in fatigue during OTS could be a reduction in muscle glycogen
                           due to overtraining [50]. Glycogen is the key energy source during moderate to vigorous
                           exercise [50]. Low muscle glycogen also results in an increase in oxidative processes and
                           a decrease in total concentrations of BCAA, as reported, leading to central fatigue [50].
                           Some studies report that, during OTS, there are lower amounts of lactate in the blood in
                           overtrained athletes compared to well-trained athletes [51,52]. Therefore, post-exercise
                           blood lactate measurement could be used as a tool to identify athletes at risk of overtraining,
                           especially if such testing were performed on a regular basis [51,52].

                           2.5. Autonomic Nervous System Hypothesis
                                Certainly, an imbalance in the autonomic nervous system, reducing sympathetic
                           activation and parasympathetic dominance, could lead to some symptoms of OTS such
                           as decreased performance, fatigue, depression, and bradycardia, but also to a reduced
                           nocturnal urinary excretion of catecholamines [4,12,43]. Generally, catecholamine excretion
                           decreases with increasing training and fatigue, returning to baseline levels during the
                           recovery period [4,53]. A reduced organ sensitivity to catecholamines could therefore be
                           an indicator of symptoms of reduced sympathetic activation [43]. Furthermore, studies
 Nutrients 2023, 15, 4916                                                                                             5 of 18




                           have stated that the effects of intense training on autonomic nervous system control may
                           be reversible, even after a week of rest [54]. Heart rate variability (HRV) monitoring could
                           therefore be an indicator of autonomic function and a predictor of overtraining [45,55].

                           2.6. Oxidative Stress Hypothesis
                                 Intense physical exercise could generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) and conse-
                           quently increase oxidative stress [56]. ROS are related to post-exercise inflammatory
                           response mechanisms and to the propagation of muscle damage with promotion of ROS-
                           induced infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages into muscle [57,58]. Neutrophils and
                           macrophages generate a free radical such as superoxide, which in turn can be converted
                           into hydrogen peroxide, which is then able to react with the superoxide in the presence
                           of a transition metal to form hydroxyl radicals [58]. Furthermore, the typical markers of
                           protein oxidation and the total oxidizing capacity were elevated, while the levels of an-
                           tioxidants such as glutathione and coenzyme Q10, and γ-tocopherol and carotenoids were
                           decreased [59–61]. Alterations in redox homeostasis have also been reported in individuals
                           with OTS; however, information on ROS generation in OTS needs further research. The
                           identification of common biomarkers for overtrained athletes could allow an adequate in-
                           tervention to prevent the progression of fatigue towards a more severe stage of overtraining
                           syndrome [59–61].

                           3. Dietary Intake in OTS
                                Overtraining syndrome, and therefore an imbalance between training and recovery,
                           can be aggravated or implied by improper nutritional intake [62–64]. Nutrition therefore
                           plays a fundamental role in maintaining correct body homeostasis, as an imbalance in
                           the quantities and proportions of macro- and micronutrients, but also an incorrect state
                           of hydration, could affect correct energy intake, the maintenance of normal physiological
                           functions, and good body composition, necessary for recovery [5]. However, there are
                           few studies in the literature on the relationship between nutrition and OTS. Some of the
                           published studies state that inadequate nutrition, pathologies, and stress factors and sleep
                           disorders [65] can lead to dysfunctions of the normal metabolic processes involved in im-
                           mune, inflammatory, neurological, hormonal, and metabolic responses [65]. For example,
                           it has already been demonstrated that overtraining syndrome can reduce an athlete’s ap-
                           petite, producing a counterproductive effect, since if the athlete presents continuous caloric
                           deficits during training, these could elevate both the stress hormone and the response
                           and production of cytokines during physical exercise, limiting the athlete [11,12,66–70].
                           Furthermore, fatigue, injury, immunosuppression, and decreased performance can occur
                           not only when energy expenditure regularly exceeds daily caloric intake but also when
                           hydration is insufficient [70–72]. In fact, incorrect hydration could have a negative effect not
                           only on performance but also on the metabolism of some macronutrients, such as glycogen,
                           which can only be stored in the muscle when bound to water in a ratio of 1:3 g [72]. It has
                           been found that even low levels of dehydration can compromise both the athlete’s exercise
                           capacity and the cardiovascular and thermoregulatory responses [73]. Optimal perfor-
                           mance, therefore, is possible only when dehydration as well as hyperthermia is minimized
                           by ingesting large volumes of fluids during exercise. Therefore, the consumption of liquids
                           in volumes similar to the amount of sweat lost results in the maintenance of important

422	                           exercise lasting only 1 h. Carbohydrate ingestion also improves exercise performance,
423	                           an effect that is independent of and additional to the prevention of dehydration [73]. A
424	                           study conducted by Candegiani et al. demonstrated how an adequate daily caloric intake,
425	                           regardless of the composition of macronutrients, can have positive bodily influences, for
426	                           example, raising salivary cortisol 30 min after waking up, improving the speed and quality
427	                           of muscle recovery, and increasing the elimination rate of muscle recovery markers, mainly
428	                           creatine kinase (CK) and lactate [74]. Therefore, an increase in caloric intake could lead to a

431

434	                           higher quality of sports performance by positively influencing both muscle recovery and
435	                           the hormonal environment.
436	
437	                           3.1. Dietary Fat
438	                                 High levels of physical activity and an inadequate or unbalanced nutritional intake are
439	                           implicated in imbalances, above all hormonal [63,75–77]. Therefore, in addition to a correct
440	                           daily caloric intake, it is also important to maintain an adequate number of macronutrients.
441	                           Each macronutrient has its own precise role, for example, the daily lipid component plays
442	                           important physiological roles, especially in the construction of cell membranes, as fuel for
443	                           exercise, as antioxidants, and as precursors of some hormones [78]. Recent studies have
444	                           shown that low-fat diets impair sports performance [79–81]. For example, a high-fat diet
445	                           has been shown in some studies to potentially reduce plasma levels of pro-inflammatory
446	                           cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1 and TNF-α, due to the anti-inflammatory action of omega-3
447	                           fatty acids [82–86]. Furthermore, increasing the amount of lipids in the diet can increase
448	                           muscular endurance without the appearance of adverse effects, especially on plasma levels
449	                           of cortisol, interferon-γ, and PGE2 [78]. Some studies state that reducing the fat content
450	                           in the diet could reduce circulating testosterone levels, implicated in dysregulation of
451	                           the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid (HPTA) axis negatively affecting health and physical
452	                           performance [84]. A study by Hamalainen et al. reports that reducing dietary fat from a
453	                           daily intake of approximately 40% of energy to a daily intake of less than 25% of energy
454	                           resulted in an approximately 15% decrease in total testosterone levels compared to a diet
455	                           with a high percentage of fat, about 41% of energy intake, and a reduction in polyunsat-
456	                           urated fatty acids [83,85,86]. Despite this, it should be emphasized that a diet rich in fats
457	                           is highly discouraged due to negative effects on the cardiovascular system, which is why
458	                           the total quantity of fats in the daily diet must comply with the guidelines provided by
459	                           the World Health Organization (WHO), in which the percentage of total lipids must not
460	                           exceed 30% of total calories, combined with an intake of saturated fatty acids of less than
461	                           about 10%, and an intake of lower trans fatty acids at 1%, favoring the consumption of
462	                           unsaturated fatty acids [87–90]. Precisely for this reason, new research has focused on
463	                           how to improve sports performance without increasing the fat component beyond the
464	                           recommended percentages, and in this case, ketone ester supplementations (KEs) seem
465	                           to be a valid alternative. Interestingly, in some studies, KEs significantly inhibited the
466	                           onset of fatigue symptoms while improving the training load tolerated by the athlete,
467	                           especially resistance exercise performance, and increasing total energy intake. Furthermore,
468	                           KEs counteracted training-induced sympathetic overdrive, as also evidenced by stable
469	                           nocturnal catecholamine production. KEs also presented a marked and positive impact
470	                           on tachycardia following exercise, thus demonstrating that KEs are a powerful nutritional
471	                           strategy that prevents the development of physiological symptoms of overtraining and
472	                           determines their overcoming [91]. Currently, medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) supple-
473	                           ments as a source of fat and as an energy source have also gained greater attention in the
474	                           sports field. MCTs could directly enter the mitochondrial level and be used for energy
475	                           production through the beta-oxidation process [92]. This process would provide the athlete
476	                           with an immediate source of fat that can be used for energy purposes, thus saving glycogen
477	                           consumption [36]. Although there are studies that state that MCTs show improved athletic
478	                           performance, other studies show side effects such as gastrointestinal disorders when taking
479	                           MCTs compared to carbohydrates [92]. Further research is therefore necessary in the field
480	                           of sports nutrition supplementation in this area.
481	
482	                           3.2. Dietary Protein
483	                                The protein component, on the other hand, is essential for the maintenance and growth
484	                           of muscle tissue [78]. Following high-intensity workouts, the ratio between protein degra-
485	                           dation and synthesis increases, resulting in a greater consumption of dietary protein [78,93].
486	                           Therefore, there is a linear relationship between protein intake and loss of lean mass dur-
487	                           ing periods of negative energy balance, so a good protein supplementation proves to be
488	 Nutrients 2023, 15, 4916                                                                                            7 of 18
489	
490	
491	
492	
493	                           an effective strategy to mitigate the loss of lean body mass [94,95]. An imbalance in the
494	                           mechanisms involved in the defense of the individual has been observed due to moderate
495	                           and severe protein imbalance [82,96]. It has been reported that diets low in protein (<20%)
496	                           or, on the contrary, abundant in protein (>60%) have been shown to impair phagocytosis
497	                           activity and the production of interleukins such as IL-2, resulting in potential damage
498	                           to the T cell system [82]. Glutamine plays a fundamental role in protein composition, as
499	                           previously mentioned. Glutamine is mainly used as fuel for lymphocytes and macrophages
500	                           for the synthesis of DNA and RNA [13,97–100]. Intense exercise can lead to depletion
501	                           of skeletal muscle stores; therefore, it has been hypothesized that glutamine depletion
502	                           may be linked to impaired immunity [99,100]. As stated in one study, a low protein in-
503	                           take can be responsible for protein loss, but in reality, even a high protein intake can be
504	                           harmful and cause an approximately 25% decrease in the amount of plasma glutamine
505	                           due to an increase in renal absorption [78]. Furthermore, the dietary protein component is
506	                           an important determinant of body characteristics; in fact, it is positively correlated with
507	                           parameters such as metabolism and body composition, and with an increase in the basal
508	                           metabolic rate (BMR), fat oxidation, muscle mass, and consequent hydration. Protein intake
509	                           is significantly but inversely related to extracellular water, i.e., it protects against water
510	                           loss, thus preventing edema [74,101–104]. Finally, growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like
511	                           growth factor-1 (IGF-I) appear to be related to healthy diet and lifestyle, while they appear
512	                           to be impaired during OTS [105,106]. IGF-1 mediates many of the actions of GHs, which
513	                           regulate growth processes, maintenance above all of lean mass but also bone mass, cel-
514	                           lular differentiation, and mitochondrial homeostasis, a process that is, in turn, key to the
515	                           metabolic processing of carbohydrates, fats, and amino acids (AAs) [107–109]. During a
516	                           fasted condition, GH primarily inhibits and reduces protein degradation by stimulating
517	                           its synthesis in muscle and other tissues [110]. This defense mechanism, to all intents and
518	                           purposes, could also be mediated by IGF-I, considering that chronic GH exposure increases
519	                           hepatic IGF-I production [111]. In order, therefore, to maintain protein homeostasis and to
520	                           support and/or prevent OTS, protein requirements for healthy endurance athletes have
521	                           been estimated at approximately 1.2-1.4 g/kg and slightly higher for endurance training
522	                           athletes up to about 1.7 g/kg [112,113]. The acceptable macronutrient distribution range
523	                           (AMDR) states that proteins can vary from 0.8 g/kg to 2.5 g/kg based on individual needs,
524	                           converted in percentage from 10% to 35% of energy, but the increase in protein requirement
525	                           and intake to date remains controversial [114,115]. As regards the integration of BCAAs,
526	                           whose imbalance appears to be a cause of the emergence of overtraining, currently, in this
527	                           case the results are not yet convincing. As stated by Gastmann et al., BCAAs, if taken
528	                           with an adequate dose of carbohydrates during prolonged physical exercise, would not
529	                           seem to determine improvements in OTS. Furthermore, high doses of ingested BCAAs
530	                           could increase the secondary production of ammonia, leading to further premature fatigue,
531	                           as BCAAs are considered the main donors of amino groups at a muscular level. Overall
532	                           results in this field are currently inconclusive and require more controlled experimental re-
533	                           search [116]. Finally, regarding the use of creatine as a sports protein supplement, currently,
534	                           despite its widespread use in this field, studies and research are still needed to explore
535	                           the topic in more depth. From what has emerged in the literature, creatine could have a
536	                           positive effect on muscle recovery, muscle hypertrophy, and strength. In a study by Wang
537	                           et al. and Ribeiro et al., the use of a higher dose of approximately 20 g per day (period
538	                           of approximately 5 days), and a subsequent maintenance dose of approximately 3 g per
539	                           day (51 days), combined with resistance training, led to hypertrophy of the skeletal muscle
540	                           mass, less fatigue, and reduction in creatine kinase in the creatine-treated group compared
541	                           to the control group [117,118].
542	
543	                           3.3. Dietary Carbohydrate
544	                               In addition to lipids and proteins, carbohydrates, according to numerous studies
545	                           conducted in recent years, play a role as the main macronutrient to support and improve
546	                           physical performance [119]. Carbohydrates, therefore, play the role of primary fuel, espe-
547	 Nutrients 2023, 15, 4916                                                                                             8 of 18
548	
549	
550	
551	
552	                           cially for the first 60–90 min of sports activity in the form of muscle and liver glycogen [120].
553	                           Similarly, after physical activity, the intake of carbohydrates supplies the muscle cells with
554	                           the fuel necessary to begin the muscle reconstruction processes. Using the energy gained
555	                           from burning carbohydrates, the muscles can absorb amino acids from the bloodstream,
556	                           initiating protein synthesis [119]. Furthermore, carbohydrates stimulate the production and
557	                           release of insulin, an anabolic hormone that plays a key role both in protein synthesis and in
558	                           the reduction of protein breakdown [120]. During exercise, muscle cell injury often occurs
559	                           with a characteristic increase in plasma creatine kinase activity and a consequent increase in
560	                           post-exercise cytokine release [121]. Furthermore, a reduction in blood glucose levels may
561	                           be linked to activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, increased release
562	                           of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and consequently cortisol, increased GH levels, a
563	                           decrease in insulin levels, and highly variable levels of adrenaline [122,123]. Several studies
564	                           in the literature suggest that carbohydrates have effects on the production of IL-6 and the
565	                           IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1ra) involved in the inflammatory cascade response to heavy
566	                           exertion, reducing their plasma levels and altering the release [98,124,125]. In addition,
567	                           the consumption of carbohydrates during physical activity appears to attenuate the in-
568	                           crease in hormones such as cortisol and GH, limiting the degree of immunosuppression
569	                           following physical exercise [123]. While increasing the amount of carbohydrates has been
570	                           shown to have predominantly positive effects on the hormonal profile, however, excessive
571	                           intake could have a pro-inflammatory role [126,127]. In fact, it could potentially induce a
572	                           pathological increase in the action of aromatase, i.e., the enzymatic system responsible for
573	                           the conversion of the androgen hormone, testosterone, into estrogen, estradiol, causing
574	                           an imbalance in the testosterone–estradiol (T/E) ratio [101,102,104,126]. Furthermore, an
575	                           excessive intake of carbohydrates could lead to an increase in lactate levels and a slight,
576	                           but not significant, increase in neutrophils [126–129]. In conclusion, the deprivation of car-
577	                           bohydrates can determine reduced and/or delayed hormonal responses, which indirectly
578	                           compromise the performance of athletes; therefore, to build excellent glycogen stores and
579	                           help rebuild muscle tissue after physical activity, a rapid and adequate carbohydrate intake
580	                           is required. If an intake of carbohydrates of less than about 5.0 g/kg/day has harmful
581	                           effects on the hormonal level and on physical performance, in order to ensure that good
582	                           muscle reserves and correct physiological functions are associated with it, carbohydrate in-
583	                           take should equal approximately 8 to 10 g/kg of body mass per day, which could represent
584	                           60 to 70% of total calories [74,106,127,130]. Furthermore, it is essential to evaluate the use of
585	                           carbohydrate-based supplements during training and sports. Among the most used supple-
586	                           ments are maltodextrins, which have been used in recent years. The effect of maltodextrins
587	                           (polymers deriving from the hydrolysis process of starches [131]) during sports practice has
588	                           been investigated in several studies, which however have presented conflicting results and

                           physiological functions and significantly improves exercise performance, even during
                           exercise lasting only 1 h. Carbohydrate ingestion also improves exercise performance,
                           an effect that is independent of and additional to the prevention of dehydration [73]. A
                           study conducted by Candegiani et al. demonstrated how an adequate daily caloric intake,
                           regardless of the composition of macronutrients, can have positive bodily influences, for
                           example, raising salivary cortisol 30 min after waking up, improving the speed and quality

                           creatine kinase (CK) and lactate [74]. Therefore, an increase in caloric intake could lead to a

                           higher quality of sports performance by positively influencing both muscle recovery and
                           the hormonal environment.

                           3.1. Dietary Fat
                                 High levels of physical activity and an inadequate or unbalanced nutritional intake are
                           implicated in imbalances, above all hormonal [63,75–77]. Therefore, in addition to a correct
                           daily caloric intake, it is also important to maintain an adequate number of macronutrients.
                           Each macronutrient has its own precise role, for example, the daily lipid component plays
                           important physiological roles, especially in the construction of cell membranes, as fuel for
                           exercise, as antioxidants, and as precursors of some hormones [78]. Recent studies have
                           shown that low-fat diets impair sports performance [79–81]. For example, a high-fat diet
                           has been shown in some studies to potentially reduce plasma levels of pro-inflammatory
                           cytokines such as IL-6, IL-1 and TNF-α, due to the anti-inflammatory action of omega-3
                           fatty acids [82–86]. Furthermore, increasing the amount of lipids in the diet can increase
                           muscular endurance without the appearance of adverse effects, especially on plasma levels
                           of cortisol, interferon-γ, and PGE2 [78]. Some studies state that reducing the fat content
                           in the diet could reduce circulating testosterone levels, implicated in dysregulation of
                           the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid (HPTA) axis negatively affecting health and physical
                           performance [84]. A study by Hamalainen et al. reports that reducing dietary fat from a
                           daily intake of approximately 40% of energy to a daily intake of less than 25% of energy
                           resulted in an approximately 15% decrease in total testosterone levels compared to a diet
                           with a high percentage of fat, about 41% of energy intake, and a reduction in polyunsat-
                           urated fatty acids [83,85,86]. Despite this, it should be emphasized that a diet rich in fats
                           is highly discouraged due to negative effects on the cardiovascular system, which is why
                           the total quantity of fats in the daily diet must comply with the guidelines provided by
                           the World Health Organization (WHO), in which the percentage of total lipids must not
                           exceed 30% of total calories, combined with an intake of saturated fatty acids of less than
                           about 10%, and an intake of lower trans fatty acids at 1%, favoring the consumption of
                           unsaturated fatty acids [87–90]. Precisely for this reason, new research has focused on
                           how to improve sports performance without increasing the fat component beyond the
                           recommended percentages, and in this case, ketone ester supplementations (KEs) seem
                           to be a valid alternative. Interestingly, in some studies, KEs significantly inhibited the
                           onset of fatigue symptoms while improving the training load tolerated by the athlete,
                           especially resistance exercise performance, and increasing total energy intake. Furthermore,
                           KEs counteracted training-induced sympathetic overdrive, as also evidenced by stable
                           nocturnal catecholamine production. KEs also presented a marked and positive impact
                           on tachycardia following exercise, thus demonstrating that KEs are a powerful nutritional
                           strategy that prevents the development of physiological symptoms of overtraining and
                           determines their overcoming [91]. Currently, medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) supple-
                           ments as a source of fat and as an energy source have also gained greater attention in the
                           sports field. MCTs could directly enter the mitochondrial level and be used for energy
                           production through the beta-oxidation process [92]. This process would provide the athlete
                           with an immediate source of fat that can be used for energy purposes, thus saving glycogen
                           consumption [36]. Although there are studies that state that MCTs show improved athletic
                           performance, other studies show side effects such as gastrointestinal disorders when taking
                           MCTs compared to carbohydrates [92]. Further research is therefore necessary in the field
                           of sports nutrition supplementation in this area.

                           dation and synthesis increases, resulting in a greater consumption of dietary protein [78,93].

                           ing periods of negative energy balance, so a good protein supplementation proves to be

                           an effective strategy to mitigate the loss of lean body mass [94,95]. An imbalance in the
                           mechanisms involved in the defense of the individual has been observed due to moderate
                           and severe protein imbalance [82,96]. It has been reported that diets low in protein (<20%)
                           or, on the contrary, abundant in protein (>60%) have been shown to impair phagocytosis
                           activity and the production of interleukins such as IL-2, resulting in potential damage
                           to the T cell system [82]. Glutamine plays a fundamental role in protein composition, as
                           previously mentioned. Glutamine is mainly used as fuel for lymphocytes and macrophages
                           for the synthesis of DNA and RNA [13,97–100]. Intense exercise can lead to depletion
                           of skeletal muscle stores; therefore, it has been hypothesized that glutamine depletion
                           may be linked to impaired immunity [99,100]. As stated in one study, a low protein in-
                           take can be responsible for protein loss, but in reality, even a high protein intake can be
                           harmful and cause an approximately 25% decrease in the amount of plasma glutamine
                           due to an increase in renal absorption [78]. Furthermore, the dietary protein component is
                           an important determinant of body characteristics; in fact, it is positively correlated with
                           parameters such as metabolism and body composition, and with an increase in the basal
                           metabolic rate (BMR), fat oxidation, muscle mass, and consequent hydration. Protein intake
                           is significantly but inversely related to extracellular water, i.e., it protects against water
                           loss, thus preventing edema [74,101–104]. Finally, growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like
                           growth factor-1 (IGF-I) appear to be related to healthy diet and lifestyle, while they appear
                           to be impaired during OTS [105,106]. IGF-1 mediates many of the actions of GHs, which
                           regulate growth processes, maintenance above all of lean mass but also bone mass, cel-
                           lular differentiation, and mitochondrial homeostasis, a process that is, in turn, key to the
                           metabolic processing of carbohydrates, fats, and amino acids (AAs) [107–109]. During a
                           fasted condition, GH primarily inhibits and reduces protein degradation by stimulating
                           its synthesis in muscle and other tissues [110]. This defense mechanism, to all intents and
                           purposes, could also be mediated by IGF-I, considering that chronic GH exposure increases
                           hepatic IGF-I production [111]. In order, therefore, to maintain protein homeostasis and to
                           support and/or prevent OTS, protein requirements for healthy endurance athletes have
                           been estimated at approximately 1.2-1.4 g/kg and slightly higher for endurance training
                           athletes up to about 1.7 g/kg [112,113]. The acceptable macronutrient distribution range
                           (AMDR) states that proteins can vary from 0.8 g/kg to 2.5 g/kg based on individual needs,
                           converted in percentage from 10% to 35% of energy, but the increase in protein requirement
                           and intake to date remains controversial [114,115]. As regards the integration of BCAAs,
                           whose imbalance appears to be a cause of the emergence of overtraining, currently, in this
                           case the results are not yet convincing. As stated by Gastmann et al., BCAAs, if taken
                           with an adequate dose of carbohydrates during prolonged physical exercise, would not
                           seem to determine improvements in OTS. Furthermore, high doses of ingested BCAAs
                           could increase the secondary production of ammonia, leading to further premature fatigue,
                           as BCAAs are considered the main donors of amino groups at a muscular level. Overall
                           results in this field are currently inconclusive and require more controlled experimental re-
                           search [116]. Finally, regarding the use of creatine as a sports protein supplement, currently,
                           despite its widespread use in this field, studies and research are still needed to explore
                           the topic in more depth. From what has emerged in the literature, creatine could have a
                           positive effect on muscle recovery, muscle hypertrophy, and strength. In a study by Wang
                           et al. and Ribeiro et al., the use of a higher dose of approximately 20 g per day (period
                           of approximately 5 days), and a subsequent maintenance dose of approximately 3 g per
                           day (51 days), combined with resistance training, led to hypertrophy of the skeletal muscle
                           mass, less fatigue, and reduction in creatine kinase in the creatine-treated group compared
                           to the control group [117,118].

                           conducted in recent years, play a role as the main macronutrient to support and improve
                           physical performance [119]. Carbohydrates, therefore, play the role of primary fuel, espe-

                           cially for the first 60–90 min of sports activity in the form of muscle and liver glycogen [120].

                           release of insulin, an anabolic hormone that plays a key role both in protein synthesis and in

                           with a characteristic increase in plasma creatine kinase activity and a consequent increase in

                           be linked to activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, increased release
                           of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and consequently cortisol, increased GH levels, a

                           in the literature suggest that carbohydrates have effects on the production of IL-6 and the
                           IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1ra) involved in the inflammatory cascade response to heavy
                           exertion, reducing their plasma levels and altering the release [98,124,125]. In addition,
                           the consumption of carbohydrates during physical activity appears to attenuate the in-
                           crease in hormones such as cortisol and GH, limiting the degree of immunosuppression
                           following physical exercise [123]. While increasing the amount of carbohydrates has been
                           shown to have predominantly positive effects on the hormonal profile, however, excessive
                           intake could have a pro-inflammatory role [126,127]. In fact, it could potentially induce a
                           pathological increase in the action of aromatase, i.e., the enzymatic system responsible for
                           the conversion of the androgen hormone, testosterone, into estrogen, estradiol, causing
                           an imbalance in the testosterone–estradiol (T/E) ratio [101,102,104,126]. Furthermore, an
                           excessive intake of carbohydrates could lead to an increase in lactate levels and a slight,
                           but not significant, increase in neutrophils [126–129]. In conclusion, the deprivation of car-
                           bohydrates can determine reduced and/or delayed hormonal responses, which indirectly
                           compromise the performance of athletes; therefore, to build excellent glycogen stores and
                           help rebuild muscle tissue after physical activity, a rapid and adequate carbohydrate intake
                           is required. If an intake of carbohydrates of less than about 5.0 g/kg/day has harmful
                           effects on the hormonal level and on physical performance, in order to ensure that good
                           muscle reserves and correct physiological functions are associated with it, carbohydrate in-
                           take should equal approximately 8 to 10 g/kg of body mass per day, which could represent
                           60 to 70% of total calories [74,106,127,130]. Furthermore, it is essential to evaluate the use of
                           carbohydrate-based supplements during training and sports. Among the most used supple-

                           alone [133]. Therefore, it is concluded that only carbohydrate supplementation in combina-
                           tion with glutamine peptide could improve the physical performance of athletes during
                           competitions.

 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the right-leg SLHB deficit as a validated injury predictor and use it to clear or flag players, when the signal appeared only in univariate analysis, the multivariable model was not significant, and left-sided results did not support it.",
 "paper": {

   "abstract": "A prospective study of 482 amateur and semi-elite Australian Rules Football players tested for single leg hamstring bridge repetitions in preseason and followed for hamstring injury through one season.
