   "tldr": "A lower preseason right-leg single leg bridge score was linked to right-sided hamstring injury in this cohort. The association was not significant in the multivariable model, so the test is a possible screening signal, not a validated predictor.",
   "methods": "Players were tested in the 2011 preseason on the single leg hamstring bridge (repetitions to failure) and dorsiflexion range, and completed a questionnaire on age, dominant kicking leg, and previous hamstring and knee injury. Injuries were confirmed by a physiotherapist or doctor and tracked weekly for one season. Data were analysed with Mann-Whitney U, chi-square, and logistic regression, with right and left injuries analysed separately.",
   "findings": "Of 482 players, 28 had a hamstring injury (16 right, 12 left). Right SLHB was lower in players with a right-sided injury (20.31 vs 25.98 repetitions, p = 0.029), and left SLHB did not differ for left injuries.    "limitations": "Only 28 injuries occurred, too few for a reliable multivariable model.    "athleteDev": "Performance Application: This is an injury-risk screen, not a performance measure.  "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 11 prospective studies (PRISMA-style search to June 2016, PROSPERO CRD42015024620) on whether MRI findings at injury or at return to play predict hamstring re-injury in athletes with acute hamstring injury.    "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2016-096790",
   "abstract": "A systematic review of 11 studies (7 low and 4 high risk of bias) on MRI findings at injury or return to play as predictors of hamstring re-injury.    "tldr": "MRI findings at injury or return to play do not reliably predict hamstring re-injury. The strongest signals are an intratendinous injury and biceps femoris involvement, but these come from underpowered studies.",
   "methods": "Eleven prospective studies were identified from 13 databases to June 2016 (PROSPERO CRD42015024620). Two reviewers screened studies, risk of bias was assessed with the Hayden consensus criteria across six domains, and data were synthesised qualitatively with a best-evidence approach because the studies were too heterogeneous to pool. A post hoc analysis used only the two studies with 20 or more re-injuries.",
   "findings": "No strong evidence for any MRI finding as a re-injury risk factor. Moderate evidence was found that intratendinous injuries (British Muscle Injury Classification, Pollock et al.) are associated with re-injury (p = 0.030), and the post hoc analysis showed a moderate to strong association with biceps femoris involvement (18% vs 2% for semimembranosus or semitendinosus, p = 0.009). Moderate evidence of no association was found for fibrosis on MRI at return to play. Re-injury rates across studies ranged from 9% to 40%.",
   "limitations": "Most included studies were small, with 4 to 41 re-injuries, which creates a high risk of missing real associations.    "practicalImplications": "A biceps femoris injury can be identified clinically, and an intratendinous injury may be easier to identify on MRI, so MRI may help estimate re-injury risk in that case.    "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: MRI at return to play showed no association with re-injury (moderate evidence), so the review does not support using an MRI at return to play as a clearance criterion.  }

   "citation": "van Heumen M, Tol JL, de Vos RJ, Moen MH, Weir A, Orchard J, et al. The prognostic value of MRI in determining reinjury risk following acute hamstring injury: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2017;0:1-10 (published online first).",
   "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2016-096790",
   "abstract": "A systematic review of 11 studies (7 low and 4 high risk of bias) on MRI findings at injury or return to play as predictors of hamstring re-injury. No strong evidence was found for any MRI finding; moderate evidence linked intratendinous injury at baseline to re-injury, and biceps femoris involvement was associated with re-injury in a post hoc analysis.",
   "tldr": "MRI findings at injury or return to play do not reliably predict hamstring re-injury. The strongest signals are an intratendinous injury and biceps femoris involvement, but these come from underpowered studies.",
   "methods": "Eleven prospective studies were identified from 13 databases to June 2016 (PROSPERO CRD42015024620). Two reviewers screened studies, risk of bias was assessed with the Hayden consensus criteria across six domains, and data were synthesised qualitatively with a best-evidence approach because the studies were too heterogeneous to pool. A post hoc analysis used only the two studies with 20 or more re-injuries.",
   "findings": "No strong evidence for any MRI finding as a re-injury risk factor. Moderate evidence was found that intratendinous injuries (British Muscle Injury Classification, Pollock et al.) are associated with re-injury (p = 0.030), and the post hoc analysis showed a moderate to strong association with biceps femoris involvement (18% vs 2% for semimembranosus or semitendinosus, p = 0.009). Moderate evidence of no association was found for fibrosis on MRI at return to play. Re-injury rates across studies ranged from 9% to 40%.",
   "limitations": "Most included studies were small, with 4 to 41 re-injuries, which creates a high risk of missing real associations. Re-injury was defined differently across studies, and only three studies adequately adjusted for confounders. The abstract refers to time to return to play, but the results in this article address re-injury only, so that abstract claim cannot be checked against the body of the paper.",
   "practicalImplications": "A biceps femoris injury can be identified clinically, and an intratendinous injury may be easier to identify on MRI, so MRI may help estimate re-injury risk in that case. The paper does not support using MRI at return to play to predict re-injury, and clinical factors may be as useful at injury.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: This is not a performance study. Staff can use it to weigh whether an MRI is worth the cost for predicting re-injury, which is a decision about injury management rather than training load.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: MRI at return to play showed no association with re-injury (moderate evidence), so the review does not support using an MRI at return to play as a clearance criterion. The paper's findings about baseline MRI and re-injury are an input to rehabilitation planning, but the review does not establish a return-to-play threshold."
